## TwinDesk 3.0: now on iPhone, iPad and any browser

https://twin-desk.vercel.app

![TwinDesk 3.0](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/InukaAsith/TwinDesk/main/.github/assets/v30-banner.jpg)

The biggest TwinDesk release so far, and the first new major version. TwinDesk now has **a native app for iPhone and iPad**, **TwinDesk Web** for any device with a browser (nothing to install), and **phones that pair with each other**: Android to Android, iPhone to iPhone, and Android to iPhone. The computers get a **Glass look**, **AirPlay on Windows and Linux**, **Tailscale**, and **five languages on every app**.

### ⬇️ Download

| Device | File |
|---|---|
| **Windows** (Intel / AMD) | [`TwinDesk-Setup-3.0.0.exe`](https://github.com/InukaAsith/TwinDesk/releases/download/v3.0.0/TwinDesk-Setup-3.0.0.exe) |
| **Windows** (ARM) | [`TwinDesk-Setup-3.0.0-arm64.exe`](https://github.com/InukaAsith/TwinDesk/releases/download/v3.0.0/TwinDesk-Setup-3.0.0-arm64.exe) |
| **Mac** (Apple silicon, M1 and later) | [`TwinDesk-3.0.0-arm64.dmg`](https://github.com/InukaAsith/TwinDesk/releases/download/v3.0.0/TwinDesk-3.0.0-arm64.dmg) |
| **Mac** (Intel) | [`TwinDesk-3.0.0-x64_Intel.dmg`](https://github.com/InukaAsith/TwinDesk/releases/download/v3.0.0/TwinDesk-3.0.0-x64_Intel.dmg) |
| **Mac** (Homebrew) | `brew install --cask inukaasith/twindesk/twindesk` |
| **Linux** (any distro) | [`TwinDesk-3.0.0-x86_64.AppImage`](https://github.com/InukaAsith/TwinDesk/releases/download/v3.0.0/TwinDesk-3.0.0-x86_64.AppImage) |
| **Linux** (Debian / Ubuntu) | [`TwinDesk-3.0.0-amd64.deb`](https://github.com/InukaAsith/TwinDesk/releases/download/v3.0.0/TwinDesk-3.0.0-amd64.deb) |
| **Linux** (Arch) | [`twindesk-bin-3.0.0-1-x86_64.pkg.tar.zst`](https://github.com/InukaAsith/TwinDesk/releases/download/v3.0.0/twindesk-bin-3.0.0-1-x86_64.pkg.tar.zst) |
| **Android** | [`TwinDesk-3.0.0.apk`](https://github.com/InukaAsith/TwinDesk/releases/download/v3.0.0/TwinDesk-3.0.0.apk) |
| **Android** (full: notification access, SMS, Accessibility) | [`TwinDesk-3.0.0-full.apk`](https://github.com/InukaAsith/TwinDesk/releases/download/v3.0.0/TwinDesk-3.0.0-full.apk) |
| **iPhone and iPad** (sideload) | [`TwinDesk.ipa`](https://github.com/InukaAsith/TwinDesk/releases/download/v3.0.0/TwinDesk.ipa) |
| **Any browser** | Turn on **TwinDesk Web** on a computer, then type `twindesk.local` |

Already have TwinDesk? The in-app updater picks the right file for your computer. Update every device you pair: 3.0 still talks to 2.5, but the new features switch on only when both sides have 3.0.

> **Windows:** the installers aren't code-signed yet (signing is on its way). If SmartScreen stops it, choose **More info › Run anyway**.
> **iPhone and iPad:** the IPA is unsigned. Install it with SideStore, AltStore or any signing tool, which signs it with your own Apple ID. An App Store release is what [sponsoring](https://github.com/InukaAsith/TwinDesk/blob/main/SPONSOR.md) pays for.

---

### 📱 TwinDesk for iPhone and iPad

![iPhone and iPad](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/InukaAsith/TwinDesk/main/.github/assets/v30-iphone.jpg)

A native SwiftUI app with the Android app's pages, and an iPhone is a phone on the computer like any other.

- **The computer's screen on the iPhone or iPad**, mirrored or as a second display, with touch, a touchpad mode, and the **Apple Pencil as a pen** with pressure, tilt and eraser.
- **Share Screen**: the whole iPhone screen in a window on the computer, every app, like presenting in a video call. Or Screen Mirroring to the computer's AirPlay receiver.
- **Files both ways** on fx2 (four parallel ranges, hashed as they stream), **Send to Computer** in the share sheet, and the computer's folder in the Files app.
- **Photos on the computer**: its Photos page shows the iPhone's photos and videos, newest first.
- **Clipboard** both ways, the **computer's notifications**, its **sound** on the iPhone, the iPhone's **camera** and **microphone*

detail.readme:
TwinDesk

Your Mac, PC, Linux box, Android phone and iPhone, working as one desk.
One mouse and keyboard for every computer. Screens, files, clipboard, notifications, cameras, calls and texts, shared.
Free and open source. No account, no cloud, and on iPhone not even an app to install.
An open-source alternative to Microsoft Phone Link, KDE Connect, Intel Unison and Synergy, in one app.


Intel Macs, Windows on ARM, .deb, Arch, NixOS and everything else: all downloads · iPhone without an app: TwinDesk Web

What's new in 3.0 · iPhone and iPad · Computers · Android · AirPlay · Every app · How it compares · Get started · Website

## What is TwinDesk? You probably own more than one computer. A work laptop and a gaming PC. A MacBook and the Windows machine you can't give up. A Linux box under the desk. And a phone that's never more than a metre away. Each one is great on its own. Together they're a mess: two keyboards, files emailed to yourself, a phone you keep picking up, the same tab opened three times. **TwinDesk turns all of them into one desk.** Push the mouse off the edge of your Mac's screen and it carries on onto the PC, keyboard and all. Copy on one, paste on the other. Drag a file across the edge and drop it there. Open the PC's apps in windows on your Mac. Turn a tablet into a second screen. Answer your phone's calls from the computer, use its camera in your video calls, and drive the computer from the couch with it. Walk to another device and **ReZume** brings the tab, the video or the document you were on with you. It's one app on every computer, so a Mac and a PC pair exactly like two Macs. Phones are full peers, not notification mirrors. And an iPhone, an iPad or any device with a browser joins by typing **`twindesk.local`**. **Looking for a Phone Link alternative?** TwinDesk does what Microsoft Phone Link does (texts, calls, notifications, photos and your phone's screen and apps on the computer), and it also works on a Mac and on Linux, with an iPhone as well as Android, and without a Microsoft account. It replaces KDE Connect and Intel Unison the same way. See [how it compares](#compare).
**🔀 Any combination**
Mac, Windows, Linux, Android, iPhone, iPad and any browser, two at a time or [all at once](#mesh). 		**📡 Anywhere**
Same Wi-Fi, a USB cable, Tailscale, or no shared network at all: Bluetooth and a direct Wi-Fi link. 		**🔒 Yours alone**
No account, no cloud, no telemetry. Devices talk only to each other, end-to-end encrypted. 		**⚡ Built for speed**
A native Rust input lane over UDP, a parallel file engine, hardware video. [How](#speed).
--- # ⬇️ Download
**🍎 macOS**
13 Ventura or later

**🪟 Windows**
10 and 11
**🐧 Linux**
X11 and Wayland, x86_64



NixOS: nix run github:InukaAsith/TwinDesk (more) 		**🤖 Android**
10 or later, phones and tablets

The full app adds notifications, texts and Accessibility; the computer can install it for you 		**📱 iPhone and iPad**
iOS 16 or later

🍺 Homebrew on macOS:
brew install --cask inukaasith/twindesk/twindesk
Update with brew upgrade --cask twindesk: TwinDesk opens again by itself if it was running, so a Mac you drive only through it gets its mouse back. The tap follows every release.

🐧 APT on Debian, Ubuntu, Mint and Pop!_OS, kept up to date by apt upgrade:

```sh sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/apt/keyrings curl -fsSL https://inukaasith.github.io/twindesk-apt/twindesk.gpg | sudo tee /etc/apt/keyrings/twindesk.gpg > /dev/null echo "deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/twindesk.gpg] https://inukaasith.github.io/twindesk-apt stable main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/twindesk.list sudo apt update && sudo apt install twindesk ```

The repository follows every release within a few hours.

Already on 2.5? The in-app updater picks the right file. Update every device you pair: 3.0 still talks to 2.5, and the new features switch on when both sides have 3.0.
Every file and older version is on the releases page.

⚠️ First launch: the apps aren't code-signed how to allow them on macOS, Windows, Android and iPhone TwinDesk is free and has no paid Apple Developer ID or Windows code-signing certificate, so macOS and Windows don't know who made it and ask once before opening it. The source is all here. **🍎 macOS** The easiest way is **Homebrew**, which installs it ready to open: `brew install --cask inukaasith/twindesk/twindesk` From the .dmg instead: 1. Drag TwinDesk into Applications and open it. macOS says it can't verify TwinDesk: click **Done** (not Move to Bin). 2. Open **System Settings › Privacy & Security**, scroll down to Security and click **Open Anyway** next to "TwinDesk was blocked". Enter your password, then click **Open Anyway** again. You do this once; updates open normally. If macOS says TwinDesk **is damaged and can't be opened**, it isn't: run this in Terminal, then open it again: ```sh xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/TwinDesk.app ``` **🪟 Windows** 1. If the browser warns that the file isn't commonly downloaded, choose **Keep** (in Edge: **⋯ › Keep › Show more › Keep anyway**). 2. When the installer shows **Windows protected your PC** (SmartScreen), click **More info**, then **Run anyway**. On Windows 11 with **Smart App Control** on, unsigned apps are blocked with no Run anyway button. The only way past it is turning it off (Windows Security › App & browser control › Smart App Control settings), and on many Windows 11 versions it can't be turned back on without reinstalling Windows. **🤖 Android** 1. Open the downloaded .apk. Android asks to allow your browser or Files app to **install unknown apps**: tap **Settings**, turn on **Allow from this source**, go back and tap **Install**. 2. If Play Protect warns about an unrecognised developer, tap **More details › Install anyway**. The **full app** (notifications, texts and Accessibility) is easiest installed by the computer over [wireless debugging](#wireless-debugging) (Phone page › Notifications from the phone): Android then lets you turn those on. Installed by hand, Play Protect may block it, and Android 13 and later grey out notification access and Accessibility as a **restricted setting**: open **Settings › Apps › TwinDesk**, tap **⋮ › Allow restricted settings**, then turn them on. **📱 iPhone and iPad** The IPA is unsigned: AltStore, SideStore or another signing tool signs it with your own Apple ID ([how](#altstore)). The first time, iOS may ask you to trust your Apple ID as a developer in **Settings › General › VPN & Device Management**. TwinDesk Web needs none of this.
--- # ✨ New in 3.0: now on iPhone, iPad and any browser

**🌐 [TwinDesk Web](#twindesk-web)**
Type `twindesk.local` in Safari, pair once, done. Screens, files, clipboard, notifications and a remote, with nothing to install. 		**📱 [iPhone and iPad app](#iphone-app)**
Every page of the Android app, native on iOS, with Liquid Glass. Pairs over Wi-Fi, USB or Bluetooth. Add it to AltStore or SideStore. 		**🤝 [Phone to phone](#phone-to-phone)**
Android to Android, iPhone to iPhone, Android to iPhone: clipboard, files, photos, notifications and screens between phones.
**🪟 Glass look**
A new default style on every computer, with your accent's glow behind the window. 		**📺 [AirPlay on Windows and Linux](#airplay)**
Mirror an iPhone, iPad or Mac to a PC, with sound. 		**🌍 Five languages, every app**
English, 简体中文, Русский, Türkçe and Português (Brasil), on computers, phones and the web.
Also new: **Tailscale** when devices aren't on the same network, **mouse and keyboard over Bluetooth** for crowded Wi-Fi, **the phone keyboard as a real USB keyboard**, **pens** (an Apple Pencil, a stylus or a drawing tablet) with pressure and tilt in screen viewers, **4K** screens, **idle links that let laptops and phones sleep**, and a round of security hardening. The full list is in the [3.0.0 release notes](https://github.com/InukaAsith/TwinDesk/releases/tag/v3.0.0). --- # 📱 iPhone and iPad: two ways in | | 🌐 **TwinDesk Web** | 📱 **The app** | |---|---|---| | **Install** | Nothing. Safari, then *Add to Home Screen* if you like | AltStore, SideStore or any signing tool, with your Apple ID | | **Best for** | Trying TwinDesk in ten seconds, a borrowed iPad, any laptop or tablet | Everyday use: background link, USB, Bluetooth, Share Screen | | **Connects over** | Same Wi-Fi | Wi-Fi, USB cable (to a Mac), Bluetooth | | **The computer's screen** | ✅ mirror or extend, touch, Apple Pencil | ✅ mirror or extend, touch, Apple Pencil | | **Files, clipboard, notifications, remote, camera, microphone** | ✅ | ✅ | | **The iPhone's own screen on the computer** | through AirPlay | ✅ Share Screen, or AirPlay | | **Photos on the computer, Shortcuts, Back Tap, Lock Screen media** | Shortcuts | ✅ | ## 🌐 TwinDesk Web: no app needed

Every TwinDesk computer can serve the iPhone app's little sibling straight to a browser. It works on an iPhone, an iPad, a Chromebook, a friend's laptop, anything with a modern browser. 1. **On the computer,** open TwinDesk › **TwinDesk Web** and switch it on. A pairing code and a QR code appear. (Mac, Windows and Linux, in one-to-one and Multi-device mode.) 2. **On the iPhone,** on the same Wi-Fi, open Safari and type **`twindesk.local`**. Or just point the Camera at the QR code. 3. **Enter the code once.** That's the pairing. The computer shows the browser in its sidebar as one more device. 4. **Optional, recommended:** Share › **Add to Home Screen**. TwinDesk then opens like an app, connects by itself, and the computer's notifications arrive as real alerts through Web Push, sent by your own computer with no server in between. What you get in the browser: - **Receive screen:** the computer's screen, mirrored or as an extra display, with touch, a touchpad mode, keyboard, sound and the **Apple Pencil as a pen** on an iPad. - **Files** both ways, and **Drop**: a chat-like place for notes, links and photos. - **Clipboard** both ways, the computer's **notifications**, **Ring, Lock and Sleep**. - **Remote:** trackpad and keyboard, a gamepad (or a real one on the computer), the phone's **camera** and **microphone** on the computer. - **Send screen** through the computer's AirPlay receiver, and **Shortcuts** actions. - Several computers on the network? The pairing page lists them all to pick from. ## 📱 The TwinDesk app for iPhone and iPad

A native SwiftUI app with every page of the Android app. On the computer, an iPhone is a phone like any other. - **The computer's screen on the iPhone or iPad,** mirrored or as a second display, with touch, a touchpad mode and the **Apple Pencil as a pen**, pressure, tilt and eraser included. - **Share Screen:** the whole iPhone screen in a window on the computer, every app, like presenting in a video call. - **Files both ways,** *Send to Computer* in the share sheet, and the computer's folder in Files. - **Photos on the computer:** its Photos page shows the iPhone's photos and videos, newest first. - **Clipboard** both ways, the computer's **notifications**, its **sound** on the iPhone, the iPhone's **camera** and **microphone** on the computer. - **Remote** (touchpad and keyboard, gamepad, voice typing) and **Media** with the computer's Now Playing on the Lock Screen. - **Wi-Fi, USB cable or Bluetooth.** Off screen the session moves onto Bluetooth, and back to Wi-Fi when you open TwinDesk. - **Shortcuts and Back Tap:** send the clipboard, send files, show the computer's screen, lock it, play or pause. - **iPhone gets a tab bar** (Liquid Glass on iOS 26), **iPad gets a sidebar** with two columns, drag and drop and keyboard shortcuts.

### Install it TwinDesk isn't on the App Store yet (that's what [sponsoring](SPONSOR.md) pays for), so you install the IPA with your own Apple ID:


1. Install [AltStore](https://altstore.io) or [SideStore](https://sidestore.io) on the iPhone. 2. Tap **Add to AltStore** (or SideStore) above on the iPhone, or add this source by hand:
`https://raw.githubusercontent.com/InukaAsith/TwinDesk/main/altstore.json` 3. Install TwinDesk from the source. It updates from there when a new version is out. With a free Apple ID, apps installed this way have to be refreshed every 7 days; AltStore and SideStore do it for you in the background. Needs iOS or iPadOS 16 or later. --- # 💻 Computer to computer

A Mac and a Windows PC. Two Macs. A gaming PC and a Linux laptop. Pair any two computers and they behave like one: one mouse and keyboard, one clipboard, files that go where you drag them, and each other's screens, apps, cameras and speakers whenever you want them. Every feature has its own page and its own switch, and nothing runs until you turn it on. ## 🖱 One mouse and keyboard Push the pointer off the edge of your screen and **keep working on the other computer**, as if they were one. Your keyboard follows the pointer, and so do Caps Lock, media keys, volume and brightness. Trackpad gestures (Spaces swipes, pinch to zoom, show desktop) carry over. Each computer's own trackpad takes its pointer back, shake the mouse to find the pointer, and a double-tap of the hotkey brings everything home. - **Where the other computer is:** drag the screens on the Mouse page to match your desk. - **Cursor lock** keeps the pointer on the computer it's on: **Scroll Lock** (F14 on a Mac), the Mouse page, or the tray and menu bar. - **Over Bluetooth on busy Wi-Fi** (new in 3.0, off by default): the pointer and keys ride Bluetooth while screens, files and the clipboard stay on Wi-Fi. ## 🪟 Move windows Hold **Right Ctrl** (**Right Command** on a Mac), grab a window and drag it past the edge of the screen. It moves to the other computer and keeps working there. Let go of it on the way back and it returns to where you grabbed it. ## 🧩 The other computer's apps, in windows of their own Open a **Windows app on your Mac** (or a Mac app on your PC) and it gets **a window of its own**, with its own Dock icon or Start-menu pin. No full remote desktop, just the app you need, next to your own.

## 🖥 Extended display and remote screen Extend your Mac onto a PC or another Mac with a **real virtual display**, or mirror it. Or bring the other computer's screen into a window and control it from there. - **Low-latency H.264 or H.265,** hardware encoding with a fallback, up to **4K**. - **Fastest, Smooth or Steady** playback, a frame-rate cap, and optional frame generation. - **Pens** (new in 3.0): a stylus, a drawing tablet or an Apple Pencil over Sidecar draws on the other computer with pressure, tilt and eraser. Real multitouch on Windows. - **Linux:** Extend on GNOME and X11, and a guide for KDE Plasma on Wayland.

## 📁 Files, shared folders and terminal **Drag files across the screen edge** and drop them anywhere, or copy with ⌃⌥C and paste with ⌃⌥V (Ctrl+Alt+C/V on Windows and Linux), into a folder or straight into the app in front. Send from the macOS Share menu or Explorer's *Send to*, or **share a folder** that shows up as a network drive on the other side. Big and small, files move on [fx2](#speed). Need a shell? `ssh twindesk` opens one on the other computer, no passwords needed. ## 📋 Shared clipboard Copy on one computer and paste on the other, instantly or when you switch over. **Pictures** go too, up to 10 MB: take a screenshot with Win+Shift+S on the PC and paste it on the Mac. Entries from password managers are skipped, and a Recent list keeps the last few things you copied.

## 📷 Camera sharing Show the other computer's camera in a window, or send it to **a webcam every app can pick**: **TwinDesk Camera** in Zoom, Teams, Meet or the browser. A computer shares its camera only when you allow it, and a popup there says who is watching. The same works with a [phone's camera](#phone-camera). ## 🔊 Sound, microphone, notifications and Wake-on-LAN Hear one computer's sound on the other, and **use one computer's microphone on the other**, each way on its own switch. See one computer's notifications on the other as native notifications. Wake a sleeping computer with Wake-on-LAN. ## 🧭 Every page on a computer | Page | What it's for | |---|---| | **Overview** | The other computer at a glance: Ring, Lock, Sleep, Bluetooth, Do not disturb, volume, its clipboard and a drop zone | | **Connection** | Nearby devices, pairing by code or QR, Bluetooth and Wi-Fi Direct | | **Share screen / Receive screen** | Extend or mirror onto the other computer, or see and control its screen | | **Apps** | The other computer's apps in windows of their own | | **Mouse / Keyboard** | The screen layout, cursor lock, the hotkey, shortcuts that follow the pointer | | **Clipboard / Notifications / File Sharing** | Each way on its own switch, with Recent, per-app rules and shared folders | | **Audio / Camera** | Sound and microphone both ways, the camera in a window or as TwinDesk Camera | | **ReZume** | Continue the other computer's tab, video or document here | | **TwinDesk Web / AirPlay & SMB** | Phones and browsers with no app, AirPlay mirroring and a folder for the Files app | | **Multi-device** | [TwinDesk Mesh](#mesh): every device at once | | **General** | Appearance (Glass or Simple, light or dark, accent), language, Tailscale, permissions, engines in use | ## 🕸 TwinDesk Mesh: every device at once

Your laptop, your desktop, the Linux box in the corner and your phone, **all connected at once**, each talking straight to the others with no hub in between. - **One mouse, every screen.** Line your devices up on the map once, and the pointer goes from the PC to the Mac to the Linux laptop to the phone. - **One clipboard.** Copy on any of them, paste on any other. The newest copy wins. - **One notification pool.** Your phone buzzes, and every computer shows it. - **Pair once, join all.** A new device paired with one computer meets the rest by itself.
What's in Mesh, and how it differs Turn it on in the **Multi-device** page, and off again any time with everything as you left it. Connecting just two devices? Keep it off: the one-to-one mode does the same with less. The one-to-one app's pages are here too: files (the fast way, over HTTPS), the Camera, the Remote, the Deck, TwinDesk iPhone, Modules and pictures on the clipboard. ReZume works while a phone is the only device connected. Not yet: the Bluetooth mouse and keyboard, and files dragged to more than one device at a time. The phone connects to one computer at a time, and Linux joins over the same Wi-Fi only. Mesh uses the tdv2 lane in Node. See [docs/mesh.md](docs/mesh.md).
--- # 📺 AirPlay receiver: mirror an iPhone to any computer

AirPlay used to stop at Apple TVs and Macs. **With TwinDesk 3.0, a Windows PC and a Linux box are AirPlay receivers too.** Open Control Center on an iPhone or iPad, tap **Screen Mirroring**, and your PC is in the list, right next to the Apple TV. Pick it, and the whole iPhone screen appears on the computer, **with its sound**. A Mac mirrors to it the same way. - **No app on the iPhone.** It's the AirPlay already built into iOS, iPadOS and macOS. - **Screen and sound,** for presenting, demos, a game on the big screen, or a video from any app. - **Video or music only:** tap AirPlay in Photos, Safari, Music or YouTube and pick the computer. - **On a Mac,** macOS has its own AirPlay Receiver; the page shows where to switch it on and the three taps on the iPhone. - **Pairs with everything else:** with the iPhone app or [TwinDesk Web](#twindesk-web), mirroring is how the iPhone shares its screen; the TwinDesk app can also do it with **Share Screen**. **Plus SMB for the Files app.** The same page shares a folder on the computer that an iPhone or iPad adds in **Files › ⋯ › Connect to Server**, so the computer's files sit right next to iCloud Drive. --- # 🤖 Android: a full peer

Most phone links stop at notifications and a file drop. In TwinDesk your Android phone or tablet is a **full peer**: it pairs like a computer and gets the same features, plus its calls, texts, photos, files, apps and camera. On the computer, the phone's **Overview** is one tap from everything: customizable **Shortcuts** (show its screen, send files, notifications, apps), **Quick actions** (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Do not disturb, torch, ring mode and volume), its battery, signal, network and storage, the latest clipboard and its most-used apps.

## 📞 Calls and messages Answer, decline and make your phone's calls from the computer. When it rings, a small window shows who's calling with **Answer** and **Decline**. With Bluetooth, the computer becomes **the phone's headset**, so you talk and listen right there. Read and reply to your texts, WhatsApp, Instagram and Telegram on **Messages**, pictures included.

## 📲 Phone apps in windows Open **single Android apps in windows of their own**, side by side with your desktop apps. Pin them to the Dock or the Start menu and use them like any other app, with your mouse and real keyboard. **Mirroring** shows the whole phone in a window instead, with touch, mouse, keyboard and its sound. Install .apk files on the phone straight from the computer.

## 🖼 Photos, phone files and Mount Browse the phone's **photos and videos**, open any of them big, save or remove one or many. **Phone Files** browses the phone's whole storage: save, upload, rename, delete, or just drop files on the page. **Shared folders work both ways.** On a Mac, **Mount** puts the phone in Finder like any drive. ## 📷 Phone camera and microphone The phone's **back or front camera** in a window on the computer or as the **TwinDesk Camera** webcam in any video call, and the phone **as a microphone** for the computer. ## 🖱 Your mouse and keyboard on the phone Push the pointer past the screen edge and it **carries on onto the phone**. Type in any Android app with your real keyboard. New in 3.0: **the phone keyboard as a real USB keyboard**, so every symbol and accent in the phone's own layout comes out right. ## 🎮 Remote and gamepad

- **Touchpad and keyboard** for the couch or a presentation, with the keys a phone keyboard lacks. - **Gamepad,** laid out like an Xbox controller. Its buttons press the keys you choose, or turn on **Real gamepad** and the computer sees an actual controller (Windows and Linux). - **A Bluetooth gamepad for any computer**, the Mac included, with no TwinDesk and no driver there. ## 🖥 Tablet as a second screen Turn a tablet or phone into an **extra monitor**. **Extend** for more desktop space, or **Mirror** to show what's on your screen. Use touch as the mouse, or switch on touchpad mode.

# ⚡ Fast by design: tdv2 and fx2

- **tdv2:** every mouse move travels on its own encrypted UDP lane, in native Rust inside the helper. A lost packet never holds back the next one, a move never waits behind a file, and nothing is allocated per move, so no garbage collector ever pauses your pointer. - **fx2:** files move in a process of their own, in parallel ranges, hashed while they stream. 10,000 small files went from a PC to a Mac in under 48 seconds. - **Quiet when idle:** with nothing in use, links stop pinging every second so laptops and phones can sleep, and every engine starts only when it's needed. - **Always compatible.** Older TwinDesk, Bluetooth, or a firewall that blocks UDP? Everything falls back by itself. General › Advanced › *Engines in use* shows what this session runs on.
tdv2 in detail: the wire, the crypto and the guarantees **Why.** Until 2.5 every mouse move rode the same TLS-over-TCP stream as everything else. On Wi-Fi, one lost packet holds back every byte behind it until it's resent (head-of-line blocking), so the pointer stuttered for 20–300 ms whenever the air got busy or a file was on its way. On top of that, each move was turned into JSON in the helper, parsed by Node, and garbage-collected. **The lane.** When both sides have 2.5, the session negotiates a UDP lane next to it (`il: {v: 1}` in hello and welcome). Each move is one small authenticated packet: ``` 'T''L' | ver | type | seq u64 | AES-256-GCM(body) | 16-byte tag MOVE: route, move number, last event number, running total x, y ``` - **Exact under loss.** Each MOVE carries the running total, not a delta, so a lost packet costs nothing: the next one puts the pointer exactly where it belongs. The last move is sent again at +8 ms and +24 ms so the pointer always lands where you stopped. - **Clicks never overtake moves.** Clicks and keys are numbered, fenced to the moves before them and sent on both the lane and the reliable session; the receiver applies them in order, exactly once. - **Secure.** Per-session keys from HKDF-SHA256, AES-256-GCM, a 64-packet replay window as in WireGuard. Anything that doesn't authenticate is dropped. - **Follows you.** The peer's address is the last authenticated packet's, so the lane follows a switch between Wi-Fi and cable. - **Prioritised.** Voice-class DSCP marking (a qWAVE flow on Windows), and Windows' Wi-Fi low-latency mode while you drive. **Native.** `native/tdfast` (Rust, C ABI) is linked into the Swift helper on the Mac, the C helper on Linux and loaded by the C# helper on Windows. Moves go from the input hook to the socket and from the socket into the OS's input without touching JavaScript. The helpers, Node's fallback lane, Multi-device and the Android app allocate nothing per move, and the Windows helper runs with the sustained-low-latency GC mode. **Fallback.** No lane (an older app, Bluetooth, UDP blocked) means input stays on the session exactly as before. General › Advanced › Input protocol lets you pick **UDP (tdv2)**, the default, or **TCP (tdv1)**. The old and new protocols side by side: [docs/protocol.md](docs/protocol.md).
fx2 in detail: the file engine - **Its own process.** A "TwinDesk Files" utility process runs its own HTTPS server, so reading, hashing and writing never block the window, the clipboard or input. - **Parallel ranges.** A large file is fetched as several byte ranges at once. - **Verified while streaming.** Every range is hashed on the way and the hashes travel with `file.end`, so a received file is checked without being read again. - **Small files fast.** Up to 16 files in flight, asynchronous writes with backpressure on every receiver, and no O(n²) queue scans. - **Hardened.** A file stops at the size it was offered with, a full disk fails cleanly, and a sender can't choose the name of a temporary file. - **Negotiated** as `fx2` in hello and welcome. An early failure falls back to the previous HTTPS path, then to chunks on the session. Bluetooth, Wi-Fi Direct and older apps keep working.

⚙️ How it works

the Electron app, the native helpers, the Rust lane and the links between devices

Each computer runs an **Electron app**, which handles the window, pairing, the link and the state machines. Next to it runs a small **native helper** for everything the OS keeps to itself: capturing and injecting input, virtual displays, gestures, window capture and native drag and drop. Inside each helper, **tdfast** (Rust) runs the tdv2 input lane. | Folder | What's in it | |---|---| | `mac/` | macOS app (Electron) | | `mac-helper/` | macOS helper (Swift): virtual display, event tap, input injection, audio, apps, SMB | | `windows/` | Windows app (Electron) and installer | | `windows-helper/` | Windows helper (C#): hooks, SendInput, Raw Input touchpad, window capture, native drag | | `linux/` | Linux app (Electron) | | `linux-helper/` | Linux helper (C): XInput2 / XTest on X11, evdev / uinput on Wayland, XRandR, window list, XDND edge strip | | `native/tdfast/` | The tdv2 input lane (Rust, C ABI), linked into every helper | | `android/` | Android app (Kotlin, Jetpack Compose); the computers drive the phone through adb and [scrcpy](https://github.com/Genymobile/scrcpy)'s server | | `ios/` | iPhone and iPad app (SwiftUI, iOS 16+): the app, the Share Screen broadcast extension and the share extension, built in CI into an unsigned IPA | | `web/` | TwinDesk Web, the browser client each computer serves at `twindesk.local` (a PWA with Web Push) | | `shared/` | Used by every app: the wire protocol, the input lane, fx2, ReZume, the Bluetooth pipe and Wi-Fi Direct links, the phone hub, shared folders, frame generation and icons | The link between two devices is one TLS session wherever it runs: on the local network, through a phone's USB cable (adb), or through **Bluetooth LE** (a GATT pipe of TwinDesk's own, `shared/blepipe.js`). When a session on Bluetooth needs bandwidth, `shared/netlink.js` brings up a **Wi-Fi Direct** group or joins a phone's hotspot, moves the session onto it, and takes it down again once nothing needs it. Beside the session run the **tdv2** UDP lane for input (`shared/inputlane.js`, `native/tdfast`), **fx2** for files (`shared/fx2-engine.js` in its own utility process) and WebRTC for screens, cameras and sound. Each is negotiated in hello and welcome and falls back by itself. Ports: TCP **47800** (the session and files), UDP **47801** (discovery), and the input lane and fx2 on ports the two sides agree on per session.

🪶 Electron, and why TwinDesk isn't a memory hog

what runs in Chromium, what doesn't, and what it costs "Electron app" often means "a browser tab that eats a gigabyte". TwinDesk uses Electron for what Chromium is genuinely best at, and keeps everything else out of it. **What Electron does here** - **The windows** you click around in: the pages, the sidebar, settings. One codebase draws the same app on Mac, Windows and Linux, which is why a Mac and a PC pair exactly like two Macs. - **Media.** Chromium's WebRTC stack gives TwinDesk hardware H.264/H.265 encoding and decoding, low-latency screen streaming, cameras and sound on every OS, battle-tested by billions of video calls. Writing that natively three times would be slower to ship and less reliable. - **The session logic** (pairing, the link, state machines) in Node, shared with every platform. **What Electron doesn't do** - **Input never touches JavaScript.** Mouse moves go from the OS's input hook to the network and back into the other OS through a small native helper (Swift on Mac, C# on Windows, C on Linux) and `tdfast`, a Rust core. Nothing is allocated per move, so no garbage collector can stall your pointer. - **Files** move in a separate utility process (fx2), started only when a transfer needs it. **Why it stays light** - **Nothing loads until you turn it on.** Every feature is off on a new install, and a feature that's off isn't even required into memory. - **Windows that aren't needed go away.** Hidden helper windows (popups, viewers, the HUD) are closed after 30 seconds of not being needed, instead of keeping a renderer alive all day. - **Event-driven, not polling.** Idle links don't ping every second, and timers run only while something needs them. In the tray on a Mac, TwinDesk measured **about 0.3% CPU** for the app and **0%** for its helper. - **It starts fast:** compiled code is cached on disk, and each window loads English plus its own language only. **What it costs.** On a MacBook Air, with the window open and an Android phone connected, all of TwinDesk's processes together used **147 MB** (resident memory, measured while writing this). Most of that is Chromium itself, the same engine your browser and chat apps already keep in memory, and it doesn't grow with how long TwinDesk runs. Want to see what your session uses? **General › Advanced › Engines in use** lists the input lane, the file engine and the connection in use right now, and why a faster one isn't, if it isn't.

🛠 Build and run

macOS, Windows, Linux, NixOS, Android and GitHub Actions You need [Node.js](https://nodejs.org) 18+ on every platform, and [Rust](https://rustup.rs) for the native input lane (without cargo the helpers build without it and Node's lane is used). ### macOS (13 Ventura or later) ```sh xcode-select --install # Swift compiler for the helper rustup target add aarch64-apple-darwin x86_64-apple-darwin cd mac npm install npm run build:helper npm start # run from source npm run dist && npm run dmg # build TwinDesk.app and TwinDesk--.dmg in mac/dist/ ``` The disk image is named after the app inside it: `TwinDesk-3.0.0-arm64.dmg` for Apple Silicon, `TwinDesk-3.0.0-x64.dmg` for Intel. Keep `arm64` and `x64` in the names on a release: the in-app updater picks the one for each Mac by them. `npm run dist:x64 && npm run dmg` (or `npm run dmg:intel`) builds the Intel app from an Apple Silicon Mac, cross-compiling the helpers and tdfast. On first launch, TwinDesk asks for **Screen Recording**, **Accessibility** and **Input Monitoring** (once; after that the General page shows each permission's status). `npm run dist` signs the app with a certificate of its own, made the first time in `~/.twindesk-signing` (keep a backup). macOS keeps permissions per signature, so with the same certificate they carry over when an update is dragged into Applications. ### Windows 10 / 11 ```bat cd windows npm install npm run build:helper :: .NET Framework's csc.exe, and tdfast.dll with cargo npm start npm run dist :: NSIS installer in windows\dist\ npm run dist -- arm64 :: the Windows on ARM installer (or `x64 arm64` for both) ``` For the arm64 lane, `rustup target add aarch64-pc-windows-msvc`. The installer adds the firewall rules (for every network profile, and one for the helper's input lane). The Setup screen, shown once, offers to fix the firewall if something changed and to install the optional Virtual Display Driver for Extend. ### Linux (X11 or Wayland) ```sh sudo apt install build-essential libx11-dev libxi-dev libxtst-dev libxext-dev libxrandr-dev libxfixes-dev cd linux npm install npm run build:helper npm start npm run dist # AppImage and .deb in linux/dist/ ``` The Setup screen walks you through the rest. On Wayland that means input access (one admin prompt, then log out and back in once). Extend on GNOME Wayland uses Python 3 with GObject and GStreamer's PipeWire plugin (`python3-gi`, `gstreamer1.0-pipewire`), which GNOME desktops already have. #### NixOS & Nix Flakes TwinDesk includes a `flake.nix` with package, dev shell, and NixOS module support: ```sh nix run github:InukaAsith/TwinDesk # run directly nix develop # development environment ``` ```nix { programs.twindesk = { enable = true; user = "yourusername"; # adds to input/uinput groups for Wayland KVM }; } ``` See [docs/nixos.md](docs/nixos.md) for full options (firewall, Wi-Fi Direct capability wrappers, virtual displays, and more). #### Testing the Linux app from a Mac `linux/scripts/vm-test.sh` runs it in a [Parallels Desktop](https://www.parallels.com) Linux VM: it copies this checkout into the VM, builds the helper, starts TwinDesk in the VM's desktop session and drives it from the Mac. ```sh linux/scripts/vm-test.sh start # sync, build and (re)start it in the VM linux/scripts/vm-test.sh shot linux.png # screenshot of its window linux/scripts/vm-test.sh log ``` ### Android ```sh cd android ./gradlew assembleRelease # JDK 17+; app/build/outputs/apk/{standard,full}/release/ ``` `standard` is the build people download. `full` adds notification access, the SMS permissions (Messages) and the Accessibility service, which Play Protect blocks in downloaded apps; the computers install it over wireless debugging, so `npm run dist` on each platform bundles the newest `android/dist/*-full.apk`. ### GitHub Actions **Build Android**, **Build Linux**, **Build Windows** and **Build AUR** (Actions tab › Run workflow) make the standard and full APKs, the AppImage and .deb, the x64 and arm64 installers with the native lane, and the Arch package. Set the `ANDROID_KEYSTORE` secret to the key the Android app is signed with (`base64 -i ~/.android/debug.keystore`): the APKs then install over existing ones, and the Linux and Windows builds carry the full Android app. **Build Windows** signs the installers through [SignPath](#code-signing): set the `SIGNPATH_API_TOKEN` secret to the SignPath CI user's API token and pick the signing policy (`test-signing`, `release-signing`, or `none` for unsigned) when running the workflow. Alternatively, to Authenticode-sign with a certificate of your own, set `WIN_CSC_LINK` to a base64-encoded code-signing `.pfx` and `WIN_CSC_KEY_PASSWORD` to its password (run with signing `none`). When `WIN_CSC_LINK` is set, the build fails if signing can't complete instead of publishing an unsigned installer.
